name: Hibernate ORM
summary: The standard object-relational mapper for Java: it maps annotated classes to tables, tracks changes to loaded objects in a session and writes them back as SQL, and implements Jakarta Persistence (JPA).
intro: You annotate plain Java classes with `@Entity`, `@Id` and association mappings such as `@ManyToOne`, and Hibernate generates the SQL to load and save them. Work happens in a session (`Session`, or JPA’s `EntityManager`). A stateful session has a persistence context, which Hibernate also calls the first-level cache: every entity loaded in it is tracked, the same row always gives the same object, and changes are found by automatic dirty checking and written when the session flushes, with no explicit `update` call. Before running a query, Hibernate flushes pending changes that could affect its result. A `StatelessSession` skips all of that: every fetch and every update is an explicit operation.

Queries are written in HQL, an object-oriented superset of JPA’s query language, or built with the criteria API; since Hibernate 6 every HQL query is compiled to a criteria query before it becomes SQL. Native SQL queries are there when HQL can’t express something. Associations should be lazy by default, and the guide is blunt that lazy fetching is the usual source of N+1 selects: fetch what a transaction needs up front with `join fetch` or an entity graph. Hibernate can export a schema inferred from the mappings, keeps an optional second-level cache shared across sessions, and talks to PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, DB2, H2 and others through their JDBC drivers. It inspired JPA, implements the latest version of it, and is governed as a Commonhaus Foundation project; version 7.4 is the latest stable series, with 8.0 (Jakarta Persistence 4.0) in development.
strengths: The most widely used JPA implementation, with mapping for inheritance, embeddables, composite keys, versioning and natural ids
Change tracking and a unit of work per session: modify loaded objects and the right `UPDATE`s run at flush
Fine control over fetching (join, batch and subselect fetching, entity graphs, fetch profiles) plus a second-level cache
Runs on many databases through JDBC dialects, and drops to native SQL when needed
limits: Lazy associations make N+1 selects easy to write; avoiding them means planning fetches per use case
The persistence context is “magical”: automatic flushes, detached entities and proxies surprise developers who don’t know the rules
A large API and configuration surface (HQL, criteria, caches, fetch strategies) with a steep learning curve
Schema export suits tests and prototypes; versioned production migrations need a separate tool

snippet.title: The N+1 select the Hibernate guide warns about, and the join fetch that fixes it
source: // one select for the books, then one more per book when its authors are touched
List<Book> books = session.createSelectionQuery("from Book order by isbn", Book.class)
// one select with a left join: authors arrive with their books
"from Book b left join fetch b.authors order by b.isbn", Book.class)

story: In 2001 Java’s official answer to persistence was the entity bean of Enterprise JavaBeans 2: heavyweight components managed by an application server. Gavin King, working with colleagues at Cirrus Technologies, started Hibernate that year out of frustration with entity beans. It mapped plain Java objects to tables instead, quickly overtook its open-source and commercial rivals, and the book Hibernate in Action, which King wrote with Christian Bauer, spread the approach.

In 2004 King and Bauer joined JBoss, later part of Red Hat, and other early contributors followed. King joined the EJB 3 expert group and persuaded it to deprecate entity beans in favour of a new persistence API modelled on Hibernate. Members of the TopLink team joined in, and the Java Persistence API 1.0 was finalised in May 2006. Hibernate became an implementation of that standard while keeping its own richer API.

Hibernate 6.0 in 2022 was a major redesign touching the APIs, mapping annotations and query language. Hibernate 7.0 in May 2025 moved from the LGPL to the Apache License and to Jakarta Persistence 3.2. The project is now governed under the Commonhaus Foundation, and its own guide admits the team’s biggest regret: not giving the explicit, persistence-context-free `StatelessSession` more attention twenty years ago.

choices.choice: Plain Java objects instead of container-managed beans
choices.why: EJB 2 entity beans tied persistence to the application server and its component model. Mapping ordinary classes made persistence testable and usable anywhere, which was the frustration that started the project.

Tracking every loaded object and flushing changes automatically meant application code could just modify objects. The cost, the team later wrote, was a loss of direct control and traps for inexperienced users.

choices.choice: Don’t pretend the database isn’t relational
choices.why: The guide says acceptable performance is impossible without acknowledging the underlying relational model, so Hibernate keeps SQL concepts such as joins, fetch plans and native queries in view.
Joining the EJB 3 expert group turned Hibernate’s design into a vendor-neutral Java standard, so code written against JPA could run on Hibernate, TopLink or others.
